newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Norway banks profitable, but reaction mixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norway banks profitable, but reaction mixed.

text.p: Norway's two biggest banks, buoyed by the country's strong economy, booked higher first-half 1997 profits on Wednesday than in the same year-ago period.
But market reaction was mixed and the shares of Den norske Bank (DnB) and Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse fell on the Oslo Stock Exchange.
DnB, the country's largest bank, said operating profits before loan losses rose 5.6 percent to 1.34 billion crowns ($173.1 million) from the first half of 1996.
Christiania, the country's number two bank, said its operating profits before loan losses were up 7.4 percent at 1.05 billion crowns.

"The operating profits before losses at DnB and Christiania did not meet expectations," said James Alexander, bank analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "The reasons are different, but both are disappointing.
"At DnB it seems to be more a matter of costs, which came in higher than we had expected, while at Christiania it seems to be revenues that are causing a worry."

DnB operating expenses totalled 2.33 billion crowns for the first six months, up 70 million or 3.1 per cent. Christiania's second-quarter net interest income came to 853 million crowns, up marginally from the corresponding 1996 period but below the first-quarter 1997 figure.
"The reduction in net interest income is a result of continued strong competition in the market," Christiania said.
In early afternoon trade at the Oslo Bourse, DnB shares were down 0.9 percent at 33.00 crowns and Christiania stock stood at 27.90 crowns, down 2.1 percent from Tuesday's closing price.
Dealers spoke of a mix of profit-taking and disappointment.

"Many investors are a bit disappointed with the results so they are selling," a dealer said. "Many feel the shares have increased a bit too much lately, so it does not come as a surprise that they are falling now."
The bottom line at both banks increased. DnB net profits edged 0.3 percent higher to 1.49 billion crowns and Christiania's equivalent figures swelled 10 percent to 1.21 billion crowns.

"The bottom lines are higher because of continuing provision reversals," Alexander said. "This is because the Norwegian economy is strong and because of possible over-provisioning in the past. I have both DnB and Christiania on a hold."

Norwegian banks emerged profitable almost three years ago from a financial crisis and have seen their accounts sweetened by provision reversals, or writebacks made possible by bad loans turning good in an improving economic climate.

"I have both banks on a buy recommendation and will not change it," an Oslo-based bank analyst said. "I think both DnB and Christiania have much to give in terms of price/earning and price/book ratios. They are both cheap bank shares on a north-European horizon."

DnB group managing director Finn Hvistendahl said: "DnB has shown healthy profits and sound progress so far this year... The accounts show that the narrowing of interest margins is abating, while income other than interest income shows a continued rise."

Following several years characterised by a continuous squeeze on interest margins, the second-quarter accounts show a total margin of 2.69 per cent for customer deposits and lending, on a level with the margin for the first quarter, DnB said.

Christiania took a different view on margins, with president and CEO Tom Ruud saying: "The net profit is at a satisfactory level, but strong competition has put further pressure on interest rate margins.
"We will put priority on profitability rather than volumes and focus on maintaining healthy margins," Ruud said.
--Oslo newsroom +47 22 42 50 41 ($ = 7.739 Norwegian Crowns)
